Let N be the eligible catalog size including the target, and r its 1-based rank within that same catalog. With 99 uniformly sampled unique competitors drawn without replacement (N≥100), the number X ranked ahead of the target is Hypergeometric(N−1, r−1, 99). Thus expected sampled HR@10 is P(X≤9) = Σ[x=0…9] C(r−1,x)C(N−r,99−x)/C(N−1,99), with impossible combinations contributing zero. Sampled rank is X+1, with expectation 1+99(r−1)/(N−1). This is the exact without-replacement reference, derived from counting sampled competitors ahead of the target.

Resolve ties using a fixed total order, such as descending score then ascending item ID, applied identically to full-catalog and sampled rankings; r counts all competitors preceding the target under that order. Candidate-dependent tie ordering invalidates this rank-only calculation. At fixed r, increasing N generally raises expected sampled HR@10 because the sample contains a smaller fraction of the r−1 competitors ahead. Across users, average these per-user probabilities; substituting an average rank or catalog size is generally incorrect.

Sampling distortion within one model differs from reversal of comparisons between models. Sampled HR@10 smooths the full-catalog indicator 1[r≤10], allowing targets outside the true top ten to score hits. For fixed N, its expectation remains monotone in r: a better rank cannot produce a lower expected sampled hit rate. Nevertheless, averaging this nonlinear transformation over different user-rank distributions can reverse model comparisons relative to full-catalog HR@10—even in expectation. This is the inconsistency emphasized by [Krichene and Rendle, On Sampled Metrics for Item Recommendation](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/); catalog-size effects alone therefore do not establish a new ranking failure.
